sampling_model.design: Randomized finite-arm instrument with \(\lambda_z=P(Z=z)>0\) for every population arm, with inference conditional on the realized positive arm counts \((n_z:z\in\mathcal Z)\).
sampling_model.units: Independent units from a law in \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal T,\mathcal C}\).
sampling_model.treatment: The realized exposure lies in \(\mathcal X=\mathcal T\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathcal C\); target levels obey exclusion and off-target levels have saturated arm-specific responses.
sampling_model.overlap: Population positivity \(\lambda_z>0\) defines every conditional arm law \(p_z\) and skeleton law \(s_z\). The separate realized-sample condition \(n_z\ge1\) is required for finite-sample calibration; an interior skeleton is used solely for the regular-face lower bound.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: When \(\mathcal C\ne\varnothing\), no nuisance function is estimated: conditional on fixed finite arm counts, off-target allocations \(\eta_z\) factor variation-independently and induce finite-fiber kernels \(K_\eta(\nu\mid\sigma)\). For every \(\mathcal C\), including \(\varnothing\), KL calibration uses the direct skeleton multinomial law and is nuisance-free.

tldr: Only selected levels of a finely recorded exposure may define meaningful interventions. Under positive-probability random assignment and exclusion restricted to those levels, the saturated target-only model has an exact quotient: the sharp law of the target potential-outcome vector is the image of a reduced response simplex that keeps target outcome cells and one off-target mass per arm. A boundary-safe right inverse removes the number and labels of off-target categories. For nonempty \(\mathcal C\), conditional on fixed finite arm counts, a rule-specific convexity inequality yields exact equality of the full and skeleton nuisance-minimax values without asserting pointwise risk domination. Separately, a reduced method-of-types confidence region has calibration independent of \( |\mathcal C| \), including the empty-\(\mathcal C\) boundary. The exact kink frontier is left as an open question.

project_justification.gap: Gabriel, Sachs, and Sjölander report the attested low-cardinality target-contrast bound coincidences. Song, Guo, Chan, and Richardson provide attested categorical potential-outcome notation. These results motivate, but under the presently attested excerpts do not establish a formal inclusion or equivalence with, the saturated target-only model studied here.
project_justification.niche: The model has common potential outcomes only on \(\mathcal T\), saturated \(R_{c,z}\) on \(\mathcal C\), and the complete law of \(Y_{\mathcal T}\) as the target. Its comparator positioning is motivation-only under the available attestations.
project_justification.fill: The quotient and its boundary-safe right inverse give sharp identification for arbitrary finite cardinalities. Internally defined structural and arm-invariant response classes admit explicit algebraic comparisons, without attribution to a published model. For nonempty \(\mathcal C\), a rule-specific convexity reduction and nuisance-invariant lift in the conditional product experiment give equality of nuisance-minimax values without pointwise risk domination. Independently, reduced KL projection gives kink-robust finite-sample coverage, including the empty-\(\mathcal C\) boundary, and polyhedral stability converts its radius to a target-set excess bound.

related_work: Gabriel, Sachs, and Sjölander \cite{GabrielSachsSjolander2025} report the attested low-cardinality target-contrast bound coincidences described in Results 1 and 3. Those results motivate the target-only quotient problem; no published-class inclusion or response-law equivalence is claimed from the present attestation. Song, Guo, Chan, and Richardson \cite{SongGuoChanRichardson2024} introduce categorical outcome, treatment, and instrument variables, potential outcomes \(Y(x,z)\), and the notation \(Y(x):=Y(x,Z)\); this is categorical potential-outcome motivation only under the attested excerpt. The common-response versus saturated comparison below is an internal algebraic result, not an identification with their published model. Sachs, Jonzon, Sjölander, and Gabriel \cite{SachsJonzonSjolanderGabriel2023} provide response-function incidence machinery; Guo and Richardson \cite{GuoRichardson2021} provide an alphabet-generic relative-entropy concentration tool. Blackwell \cite{Blackwell1953} supplies the experiment-comparison template, while the unknown allocation kernel necessitates nuisance-minimax rather than pointwise comparison. Hoffman \cite{Hoffman1952} and Li \cite{Li1993} supply generic polyhedral error-bound tools. Levis et al. \cite{LevisBonviniZengKeeleKennedy2025} and Gafarov \cite{Gafarov2025} locate the active-facet inference problem but do not settle the target-specific kink frontier. Boushehrian et al. \cite{BoushehrianBadriAkbariKiyavash2026} show why exponential dependence on substantive support can remain after irrelevant off-target cardinality is removed.
technical_internal_limitation: The structural-form transfer and arm-invariant response-type bijection are internally defined algebraic constructions and are not attributed to the published Gabriel or Song model classes. The present attestations do not support a published-model inclusion or equivalence claim. The method-of-types radius is deliberately elementary and may be larger than the polynomial Chernoff calibration of Guo and Richardson; the contribution is the target-specific quotient that removes \( |\mathcal C| \), not a new multinomial tail inequality. The nuisance-minimax comparison and regular-face lower bound are confined to nonempty \(\mathcal C\); the former is additionally confined to the finite count experiment conditional on fixed arm counts and is not a pointwise domination statement. The exact smallest Hoffman constant and the nonregular kink law are not presupposed, and no additional rate theorem is introduced here.
honest_scope: The equality of full and reduced identified images is sharp and includes an explicit boundary-safe right inverse for the separately defined saturated target-only model. The available Gabriel and Song attestations are used only for the narrow statements recorded on their cited nodes; no published-class inclusion, response-law equivalence, or strict extension is claimed. The structural-form and arm-invariant bijection lemmas are internally defined algebraic constructions. For nonempty \(\mathcal C\), the finite-count nuisance-minimax theorem and regular-face lower bound remain separate theorem obligations; finite-sample whole-set coverage and the finite Hoffman certificate also include the empty-\(\mathcal C\) boundary. The condition \(\lambda_z>0\) only makes population conditional arm laws well defined, whereas \(n_z\ge1\) concerns the realized conditional experiment. The exact face-by-face minimax law and an adaptive attaining procedure at dual ties remain the open kink question. When \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\), \(m=2\), and \(|\mathcal T|=2\), the construction reduces to the classical Balke--Pearl response-type program.

definitions.name: Armwise off-target refinement
definitions.construction: For each reduced atom \(r=((x_z(r))_z,y_{\mathcal T}(r))\) drawn with mass \(q_r\), refine independently over \(z\). If \(x_z(r)=t\in\mathcal T\), set \(X_z=t\), retain \(Y_t=y_t(r)\), and set the unused coordinates \(R_{c,z}\) to zero. If \(x_z(r)=\star\), draw \((C_z,V_z)\sim\eta_z\), set \(X_z=C_z\), set \(R_{C_z,z}=V_z\), and set the other unused \(R_{c,z}\) to zero. Mixing these full atoms defines \(\mathfrak R_p(q)\); when \(s_z(\star)=0\), use any fixed boundary allocation because the corresponding branch has zero mass. Observed outcomes are assigned only by the target rule \(Y=Y_t\) on \(\{X=t\}\) and the arm-specific rule \(Y=R_{c,z}\) on \(\{X=c,Z=z\}\).

definitions.name: Exact response-type and linear-program certificate
definitions.construction: Enumerate the \(36\) reduced columns \( (x_1,x_2,y_a,y_b)\in\{a,b,\star\}^2\times\{0,1\}^2\), the \(144\) saturated columns \( (x_1,x_2,y_a,y_b,r_{c,1},r_{c,2})\in\{a,b,c\}^2\times\{0,1\}^4\), and the \(72\) common-response columns \( (x_1,x_2,y_a,y_b,r_c)\in\{a,b,c\}^2\times\{0,1\}^3\). For each list form its zero-one observed-cell incidence matrix \(G\), impose \(G\omega=p^{\mathrm w}\), \(\omega\ge0\), and \(\mathbf 1^\top\omega=1\), and minimize and maximize \(\sum_f\omega_f(y_b(f)-y_a(f))\). In the saturated program the lower endpoint is attained by mass \(1/2\) on each of \((a,a,0,0,0,0)\) and \((c,c,1,0,1,0)\), while the upper endpoint is attained by mass \(1/2\) on each of \((a,a,0,1,0,0)\) and \((c,c,0,1,1,0)\). The valid inequalities \(\tau\le1\) and \(\tau\ge-E[Y_a]\ge-1/2\), where \(P(Y_a=0)\ge P(X_1=a\text{ or }X_2=a)\ge1/2\), certify those saturated optima. Under the common-response restriction the lower endpoint is attained by mass \(1/2\) on each of \((c,a,0,0,1)\) and \((a,c,0,0,0)\), and the upper endpoint by the same two exposure-response columns with \(y_b=1\). The observed constraints make \(\{X_1=c,r_c=1\}\) and \(\{X_2=c,r_c=0\}\) disjoint events of total probability one and force \(Y_a=0\), certifying \(0\le\tau\le1\).

statements.statement: For every \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal T,\mathcal C}\) with \(\lambda_z=P(Z=z)>0\) for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\), observed conditional arm law \(p\), and skeleton \(s\), \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm F}(p)=\Theta(s)\). More precisely, \(A\kappa_{\#}\pi=s\) and \(B\kappa_{\#}\pi=B_{\mathrm F}\pi\) for every feasible full law \(\pi\); conversely, for every \(q\in F(s)\), the explicit refinement satisfies \(A_{\mathrm F}\mathfrak R_p(q)=p\), \(\kappa_{\#}\mathfrak R_p(q)=q\), and \(B_{\mathrm F}\mathfrak R_p(q)=Bq\), including every zero-\(\star\)-mass boundary. Hence the sharp set and the dimensions \(|\mathcal R|=(|\mathcal T|+1)^m2^{|\mathcal T|}\) and \(md\) are independent of \(|\mathcal C|\).
statements.proof_tex:
Write a full response type as
\[
f=(x_{\mathcal Z},y_{\mathcal T},r_{\mathcal C,\mathcal Z})
\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm F}.
\]
Because all potential variables have finite support, the given causal law \(P\) induces the probability vector
\[
\pi^P=\operatorname{law}_P(X_{\mathcal Z},Y_{\mathcal T},R_{\mathcal C,\mathcal Z})
\in\Delta^{|\mathcal R_{\mathrm F}|-1}.
\]
For a target cell, randomization, exposure consistency, target exclusion, and target-outcome consistency give
\[
(A_{\mathrm F}\pi^P)_{z,(t,y)}
=P(X_z=t,Y_t=y)
=P(X=t,Y=y\mid Z=z)
=p_z(t,y).
\]
For an off-target cell, randomization, exposure consistency, and off-target-outcome consistency analogously give
\[
(A_{\mathrm F}\pi^P)_{z,(c,y)}
=P(X_z=c,R_{c,z}=y)
=P(X=c,Y=y\mid Z=z)
=p_z(c,y).
\]
Every conditioning operation is valid because \(\lambda_z>0\).  Thus \(A_{\mathrm F}\pi^P=p\), so the full feasible fiber is nonempty.

We first prove the outer inclusion by a pushforward argument.  Let \(\pi\in\Delta^{|\mathcal R_{\mathrm F}|-1}\) satisfy \(A_{\mathrm F}\pi=p\), and put \(q=\kappa_{\#}\pi\).  Since a pushforward of a probability measure is a probability measure, \(q\in\Delta^{|\mathcal R|-1}\).  For \(z\in\mathcal Z\), \(t\in\mathcal T\), and \(y\in\mathcal Y\), the definitions of \(A\) and \(\kappa\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Aq)_{z,(t,y)}
&=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}q_r
  \mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=t,\ y_t(r)=y\}\\
&=\sum_{f\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm F}}\pi_f
  \mathbf 1\{x_z(f)=t,\ y_t(f)=y\}\\
&=(A_{\mathrm F}\pi)_{z,(t,y)}\\
&=p_z(t,y)=s_z(t,y).
\end{aligned}
\]
The incidence equality is algebraic.  Its causal interpretation follows from randomization, exposure consistency, target exclusion, and target-outcome consistency: positivity of \(\lambda_z\) permits conditioning and
\[
p_z(t,y)=P(X_z=t,Y_t=y).
\]
For the collapsed row, disjointness of \(\mathcal T\) and \(\mathcal C\), binary outcome support, and the definition of \(A_{\mathrm F}\) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Aq)_{z,\star}
&=\sum_f\pi_f\mathbf 1\{x_z(f)\in\mathcal C\}\\
&=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}
  (A_{\mathrm F}\pi)_{z,(c,y)}\\
&=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}p_z(c,y)
=s_z(\star).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(Aq=s\), so \(q\in F(s)\).  Moreover, \(\kappa\) retains the complete vector \(y_{\mathcal T}\).  Consequently, for every \(y_{\mathcal T}\in\mathcal Y^{\mathcal T}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Bq)_{y_{\mathcal T}}
&=\sum_f\pi_f\mathbf 1\{y_{\mathcal T}(f)=y_{\mathcal T}\}\\
&=(B_{\mathrm F}\pi)_{y_{\mathcal T}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm F}(p)\subseteq\Theta(s)\).

We next prove attainability by the explicit right inverse.  Fix \(q\in F(s)\).  Conditional on a reduced atom
\[
r=((x_z(r))_{z\in\mathcal Z},y_{\mathcal T}(r)),
\]
perform the refinement in \(\mathfrak R_p\): whenever \(x_z(r)=\star\), sample \((C_z,V_z)\) according to \(\eta_z\), set \(X_z=C_z\) and \(R_{C_z,z}=V_z\), and fill every unused off-target response coordinate with zero; when \(x_z(r)=t\in\mathcal T\), set \(X_z=t\) and again fill unused off-target coordinates with zero.  The draws may be taken independently across the finitely many arms conditional on \(r\).  Let
\[
\pi=\mathfrak R_p(q).
\]
Every full atom generated from \(r\) collapses back to \(r\).  Hence, by conditioning on \(r\),
\[
\kappa_{\#}\mathfrak R_p(q)=q,
\qquad
B_{\mathrm F}\mathfrak R_p(q)=Bq.
\]
For a target cell, the refinement adds no randomness relevant to the incidence indicator, and therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(A_{\mathrm F}\pi)_{z,(t,y)}
&=\sum_rq_r\mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=t,\ y_t(r)=y\}\\
&=(Aq)_{z,(t,y)}=s_z(t,y)=p_z(t,y).
\end{aligned}
\]
For an off-target cell, conditional independence is more than is needed; the marginal refinement at arm \(z\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(A_{\mathrm F}\pi)_{z,(c,y)}
&=\sum_rq_r\mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=\star\}\eta_z(c,y)\\
&=(Aq)_{z,\star}\eta_z(c,y)\\
&=s_z(\star)\eta_z(c,y).
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(s_z(\star)>0\), the definition of \(\eta_z\) makes the last quantity \(p_z(c,y)\).  If \(s_z(\star)=0\), then nonnegativity of \(q\) and
\[
0=(Aq)_{z,\star}
=\sum_rq_r\mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=\star\}
\]
imply that every reduced atom having \(x_z(r)=\star\) has zero \(q\)-mass.  Nonnegativity of the observed cells and
\[
0=s_z(\star)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C,y\in\mathcal Y}p_z(c,y)
\]
also imply \(p_z(c,y)=0\) for each \((c,y)\).  Thus the displayed incidence equality holds for every fixed boundary choice of \(\eta_z\).  If \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\), the sum defining \(s_z(\star)\) is zero and no positive-mass \(\star\)-branch occurs, so the singleton convention is sufficient.

It remains to verify that the constructed table is attainable in the maintained causal model.  Draw the full response type with law \(\pi\), draw \(Z\) independently with probabilities \((\lambda_z)_z\), set \(Y_{t,z}=Y_t\), put \(X=X_Z\), and define
\[
Y=\begin{cases}
Y_t,&X=t\in\mathcal T,\\
R_{c,Z},&X=c\in\mathcal C.
\end{cases}
\]
This finite construction satisfies randomization, target exclusion, exposure consistency, target-outcome consistency, and off-target-outcome consistency.  The preceding cell equations give \(A_{\mathrm F}\pi=p\).  Thus every \(Bq\in\Theta(s)\) is attained by a law in \(\mathcal M_{\mathcal T,\mathcal C}\), proving
\[
\mathcal I_{\mathrm F}(p)=\Theta(s).
\]
This is equality of the causal identified set and the observed-law functional, not a definition of the former; because every point on the right has just been attained, the equality is sharp rather than merely an outer bound.

A reduced atom has \((|\mathcal T|+1)^m\) possible exposure-response vectors and \(2^{|\mathcal T|}\) possible target-outcome vectors.  Therefore
\[
|\mathcal R|=(|\mathcal T|+1)^m2^{|\mathcal T|}.
\]
The map \(A\) records \(d=2|\mathcal T|+1\) cells in each of \(m\) arms, so its declared codomain has dimension \(md\).  Neither number involves \(|\mathcal C|\).
statements.justification: The theorem gives an exact, boundary-safe quotient and right inverse for the separately defined saturated target-only response model.
statements.gap: Published low-cardinality coarsening results motivate the target-only problem, but the currently attested excerpts do not establish a formal inclusion or equivalence between their published NPSEMs and the model defined here.
statements.consumer: Dose, adherence, and Mendelian-randomization studies may retain many irregular realized exposure levels without enlarging the identification computation for a selected target contrast.

statements.statement: If \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\), \(m=2\), and \(\mathcal T=\{a,b\}\), then \(\Theta(s)\) is the classical binary response-type polytope and the extrema of \(\tau=E[Y_b-Y_a]\) are the Balke--Pearl sharp bounds.
statements.justification: The reduction is the required sanity check against the canonical binary instrumental-variable model.
statements.gap: This is a known special case and is included as a validation result rather than a novelty claim.
statements.consumer: Implementers can unit-test the reduced incidence matrix against published Balke--Pearl formulas.
statements.proof_tex:
Relabel the two elements of \(\mathcal Z\) as \(0\) and \(1\); this is only a bijective change of indices. Put \(x_0=a\) and \(x_1=b\). The positive-arm-probability assumption makes both conditional arm laws well defined. We first verify feasibility from the maintained causal model rather than assuming it. Because \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\), each \(X_z\) takes values in \(\mathcal T\). Let \(q^P\) be the joint law of \((X_0,X_1,Y_a,Y_b)\), embedded in \(\Delta^{|\mathcal R|-1}\) by assigning zero mass to every reduced type with a \(\star\) coordinate. Target exclusion makes \((Y_a,Y_b)\) a single response vector not indexed by the assigned arm. For every \(t\in\mathcal T\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}\), randomization, exposure consistency, and target-outcome consistency give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Aq^P)_{z,(t,y)}
&=P(X_z=t,Y_t=y)\\
&=P(X_z=t,Y_t=y\mid Z=z)\\
&=P(X=t,Y=y\mid Z=z)\\
&=s_z(t,y).
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses \(Z\perp\!\!\!\perp(X_{\mathcal Z},Y_{\mathcal T})\); the third holds almost surely on \(\{Z=z,X_z=t\}\). Also, by the definition of the skeleton law, for each arm \(z\),
\[
s_z(\star)=\sum_{c\in\varnothing}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}p_z(c,y)=0=(Aq^P)_{z,\star}.
\]
Thus \(Aq^P=s\), so \(q^P\in F(s)\) and the fiber is nonempty.

We next identify the support of every feasible reduced law. 
If \(q\in F(s)\), then the definition of \(F(s)\), followed by the \(\star\)-row in the definition of \(A\), yields
\[
0=s_z(\star)=(Aq)_{z,\star}
 =\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}q_r\mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=\star\}.
\]
Every summand is nonnegative because \(q\) belongs to a probability simplex. Hence \(q_r=0\) whenever \(x_z(r)=\star\). Applying this argument for both arms proves that every \(q\in F(s)\) is supported on
\[
\mathcal R_0=\mathcal T^{\{0,1\}}\times\{0,1\}^{\mathcal T},
\qquad |\mathcal R_0|=2^2\,2^2=16.
\]

Define a bijection \(\iota:\mathcal R_0\to\{0,1\}^4\) by
\[
\iota(r)=(d_0,d_1,u_0,u_1),\qquad
d_z=\mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=b\},\quad u_0=y_a(r),\quad u_1=y_b(r).
\]
Thus \((d_0,d_1)\) is the binary response function from assignment to received exposure and \((u_0,u_1)\) is the binary response function from exposure to outcome. Push \(q\) forward through \(\iota\), writing the resulting mass as \(\widetilde q_{d_0d_1u_0u_1}\). For \(y,d,z\in\{0,1\}\), define the observed-law coordinate
\[
\pi_{yd.z}=s_z(x_d,y).
\]
The target-cell row of \(Aq=s\) then becomes, term by term,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{yd.z}
&=s_z(x_d,y)\\
&=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_0}q_r
  \mathbf 1\{x_z(r)=x_d,\ y_{x_d}(r)=y\}\\
&=\sum_{d_0,d_1,u_0,u_1}
  \widetilde q_{d_0d_1u_0u_1}
  \mathbf 1\{d_z=d,\ u_d=y\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are exactly the classical binary instrumental-variable response-type equations. Conversely, any \(\widetilde q\in\Delta^{15}\) satisfying these equations defines, through \(\iota^{-1}\), a distribution on \(\mathcal R_0\); extending it by zero to \(\mathcal R\) satisfies every target-cell equation and also every \(\star\)-equation of \(Aq=s\). Therefore pushforward by \(\iota\) is an affine bijection
\[
F(s)\longleftrightarrow\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{IV}}(\pi).
\]
This establishes equality of the feasible response-type polytopes, rather than merely an outer relaxation.

It remains to check that the target maps agree. For \((u_0,u_1)\in\{0,1\}^2\), the definition of \(B\) and the bijection above give
\[
(Bq)_{(u_0,u_1)}
=\sum_{d_0,d_1}\widetilde q_{d_0d_1u_0u_1}.
\]
Consequently \(\Theta(s)=BF(s)\) is exactly the outcome-response-law image of the classical fiber. The causal contrast associated with a feasible response law is
\[
\tau(q)=E_q[Y_b-Y_a]
=\sum_{d_0,d_1,u_0,u_1}
 \widetilde q_{d_0d_1u_0u_1}(u_1-u_0).
\]
This causal quantity is distinct from the observed-law functionals \(L_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)\) and \(U_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)\), which depend only on the eight coordinates \(\pi_{yd.z}=s_z(x_d,y)\).

By the cited Balke--Pearl binary instrumental-variable linear-programming result, the minimum and maximum of the last display over \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{IV}}(\pi)\) are, respectively,
\[
L_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)=\max\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{11.1}-1,\\
&\pi_{00.1}+\pi_{11.1}-1,\\
&\pi_{11.0}+\pi_{00.1}-1,\\
&\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{11.0}-1,\\
&2\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{11.0}+\pi_{10.1}+\pi_{11.1}-2,\\
&\pi_{00.0}+2\pi_{11.0}+\pi_{00.1}+\pi_{01.1}-2,\\
&\pi_{10.0}+\pi_{11.0}+2\pi_{00.1}+\pi_{11.1}-2,\\
&\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{01.0}+\pi_{00.1}+2\pi_{11.1}-2
\end{aligned}\right\},
\]
and
\[
U_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)=\min\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&1-\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{01.1},\\
&1-\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{10.1},\\
&1-\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{10.0},\\
&1-\pi_{01.1}-\pi_{10.1},\\
&2-2\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{10.1}-\pi_{11.1},\\
&2-\pi_{01.0}-2\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{00.1}-\pi_{01.1},\\
&2-\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{11.0}-2\pi_{01.1}-\pi_{10.1},\\
&2-\pi_{00.0}-\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{01.1}-2\pi_{10.1}
\end{aligned}\right\}.
\]
The construction of \(q^P\) above proves that \(F(s)\), and hence \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{IV}}(\pi)\), is nonempty. Since the latter is the intersection of a finite-dimensional probability simplex with finitely many closed affine equalities, it is compact. Thus both extrema are attained. Convexity of the fiber and linearity of \(\tau\) further show that every value between the two endpoints is attained by a convex combination of an endpoint minimizer and an endpoint maximizer. Hence the sharp identified interval is
\[
\{\tau(q):q\in F(s)\}
=[L_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi),U_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)],
\]
To verify causal sharpness rather than only linear-program sharpness, take any \(q\in F(s)\), draw its response type independently of \(Z\), give \(Z\) its observed probabilities \((\lambda_0,\lambda_1)\), set \(Y_{t,z}=Y_t\), \(X=X_Z\), and \(Y=Y_X\). This full law satisfies randomization, target exclusion, exposure consistency, and target-outcome consistency, and the displayed incidence equations show that its observed skeleton law is \(s\). It realizes target law \(Bq\). Conversely, the construction of \(q^P\) shows that every compatible full law induces a point of \(F(s)\). Therefore the interval in the last display is sharp for the causal contrast, not merely an outer bound, which proves the theorem. The only positivity used is \(\lambda_z>0\) to define each conditional arm law; there is no division by a response-cell probability and no limiting or boundary argument.

statements.statement: For \(m\ge2\) and nonempty \(\mathcal C\), the common-response restriction \(R_{c,z}=R_c\) defines a strict submodel \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{common}}\subsetneq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sat}}\). For \(p^{\mathrm w}\) on arms \(\{1,2\}\), the response-type certificate \(\mathfrak C^{\mathrm w}\) exhaustively enumerates \(|\mathcal R|=36\), \(|\mathcal R_{\mathrm F}|=144\) under \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sat}}\), and \(72\) types under \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{common}}\). Its feasible primal mixtures and valid endpoint inequalities certify \(\tau\in[-1/2,1]\) under \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sat}}\) and \(\tau\in[0,1]\) under \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{common}}\).
statements.proof_tex:
By definition, every common-response law is saturated, so
\[
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{common}}\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sat}}.
\]
The inclusion is strict when \(m\ge2\) and \(\mathcal C\ne\varnothing\).  Choose \(c\in\mathcal C\) and distinct arms \(z,z'\), and take a degenerate response type with
\[
X_u=c\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal Z,
\qquad R_{c,z}=0,
\qquad R_{c,z'}=1.
\]
Assign arbitrary fixed values to every other response coordinate.  Draw \(Z\) independently with positive arm probabilities, set \(Y_{t,u}=Y_t\), put \(X=X_Z\), and set \(Y=R_{c,Z}\).  Randomization, target exclusion, exposure consistency, and off-target-outcome consistency follow directly; target-outcome consistency is vacuous because \(X=c\) almost surely.  The resulting full causal law belongs to \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sat}}\) but violates the almost-sure equality required by \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{common}}\), proving strict inclusion.

Now specialize to the witness.  Ordering coordinates as in the certificate, direct Cartesian-product enumeration gives
\[
|\{a,b,\star\}^{\{1,2\}}\times\{0,1\}^{\{a,b\}}|
=3^2 2^2=36,
\]
\[
|\{a,b,c\}^{\{1,2\}}\times\{0,1\}^{\{a,b\}}
\times\{0,1\}^{\{c\}\times\{1,2\}}|
=3^2 2^2 2^2=144,
\]
and
\[
|\{a,b,c\}^{\{1,2\}}\times\{0,1\}^{\{a,b\}}
\times\{0,1\}^{\{c\}}|
=3^2 2^2 2=72.
\]
Each factor ranges over its entire finite support, so these lists are exhaustive.  In particular, the certificate's linear programs expose every deterministic column and their probability-simplex mixtures expose every response-type law.

The quotient theorem also supplies a stronger cardinality check.  For any finite off-target alphabet, any full observed law with skeleton \(s\), and any direction \(h\in\mathbb R^{2^{|\mathcal T|}}\), compactness of the finite simplices and \(\mathcal I_{\mathrm F}(p)=\Theta(s)\) imply
\[
\max_{\substack{\pi\ge0,\ \mathbf 1^\top\pi=1\\A_{\mathrm F}\pi=p}}
h^\top B_{\mathrm F}\pi
=
\max_{\substack{q\ge0,\ \mathbf 1^\top q=1\\Aq=s}}
h^\top Bq,
\]
and similarly for minima.  Thus checking arbitrary support directions across different finite refinements of the same skeleton must give exact equality; in the witness the reduced side uses the enumerated \(36\) columns.

For the saturated lower endpoint, place mass \(1/2\) on each of the full types
\[
(a,a,0,0,0,0),
\qquad
(c,c,1,0,1,0),
\]
where the coordinates are \((x_1,x_2,y_a,y_b,r_{c,1},r_{c,2})\).  The first atom produces \((a,0)\) in both arms; the second produces \((c,1)\) in arm \(1\) and \((c,0)\) in arm \(2\).  Their mixture therefore has observed law \(p^{\mathrm w}\), and its contrast is
\[
\tau=\tfrac12(0-0)+\tfrac12(0-1)=-\tfrac12.
\]
For the upper endpoint, place mass \(1/2\) on each of
\[
(a,a,0,1,0,0),
\qquad
(c,c,0,1,1,0).
\]
This has the same observed law and \(\tau=1\).

We certify that no saturated mixture exceeds these endpoints.  Binary support gives
\[
0\le E(Y_a),E(Y_b)\le1,
\qquad
\tau=E(Y_b)-E(Y_a)\le1.
\]
The two observed target cells and randomization plus target consistency give
\[
P(X_1=a,Y_a=0)=P(X_2=a,Y_a=0)=\tfrac12.
\]
Thus
\[
P(Y_a=0)
\ge P(X_1=a\ \text{or}\ X_2=a)
\ge\tfrac12,
\]
so \(E(Y_a)\le1/2\).  Since \(E(Y_b)\ge0\),
\[
\tau\ge-E(Y_a)\ge-\tfrac12.
\]
The two feasible mixtures attain the two valid inequalities.  The feasible response-law set is convex and \(\tau\) is linear, so mixing the two endpoint laws attains every intermediate value.  The saturated sharp interval is therefore exactly \([-1/2,1]\).

Under the common-response restriction write a type as \((x_1,x_2,y_a,y_b,r_c)\).  The mixture with mass \(1/2\) on each of
\[
(c,a,0,0,1),
\qquad
(a,c,0,0,0)
\]
generates \(p^{\mathrm w}\) and has \(\tau=0\).  Replacing both displayed \(y_b\)-coordinates by one leaves the observed law unchanged and gives \(\tau=1\).

For optimality, define
\[
E_1=\{X_1=c,R_c=1\},
\qquad
E_2=\{X_2=c,R_c=0\}.
\]
The observed off-target cells imply \(P(E_1)=P(E_2)=1/2\).  Because \(R_c\) is binary and common across arms, \(E_1\cap E_2=\varnothing\); hence \(E_1\cup E_2\) has probability one.  On \(E_1\), the zero arm-2 probability of exposure \(b\) and the zero cell \(p^{\mathrm w}_2(c,1)\) imply \(X_2=a\) almost surely.  The zero cell \(p^{\mathrm w}_2(a,1)\), together with target consistency, then implies \(Y_a=0\) on \(E_1\).  Symmetrically, on \(E_2\), the zero arm-1 probability of exposure \(b\) and the zero cell \(p^{\mathrm w}_1(c,0)\) imply \(X_1=a\), and \(p^{\mathrm w}_1(a,1)=0\) implies \(Y_a=0\).  Therefore \(Y_a=0\) almost surely.  Binary support now gives
\[
0\le\tau=E(Y_b)\le1.
\]
The two common-response mixtures attain both endpoints while leaving the observed law fixed.  Convex mixtures attain every intermediate value, so the common-response sharp interval is \([0,1]\).  Its strict difference from \([-1/2,1]\) proves that saturated arm-specific off-target responses are a genuine relaxation of the internally defined common-response benchmark.
statements.justification: The exact witness proves internally that common off-target responses form a strict restriction of the saturated arm-specific model and can yield different target-contrast bounds.
statements.gap: This proposition is an internal comparison between \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{common}}\) and \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{sat}}\); no equivalence with a cited published model is asserted.
statements.consumer: The witness is an exact regression test for response-type software and for the right-inverse implementation.

statements.statement: If \(\mathcal C\ne\varnothing\), then conditional on \((n_z:z\in\mathcal Z)\), the likelihood of \(N\) under every \((q,\eta)\) factors as \(\prod_{z\in\mathcal Z}L_z(N_z;(Aq)_z,\eta_z)\) in Definition \(\mathrm{def:skeleton\mbox{-}factorization}\). The parameter space is the Cartesian product \(\{q:q\in\Delta^{|\mathcal R|-1}\}\times\mathcal E_{\mathcal C}^m\); conditional on \(S\), the off-target allocation counts depend on \(\eta\) but not on \(q\).
statements.proof_tex:
Fix the arm totals as required by the fixed-arm-count assumption. Given \((q,\eta)\), let \(s=Aq\).  The quotient refinement and the two consistency assumptions imply that one observation in arm \(z\) has full-cell probabilities
\[
g_z(t,y)=s_z(t,y),\quad t\in\mathcal T,
\qquad
g_z(c,y)=s_z(\star)\eta_z(c,y),\quad c\in\mathcal C.
\]
Their sum is one because \(s_z\in\Delta^{d-1}\) and \(\sum_{c,y}\eta_z(c,y)=1\) when \(\mathcal C\ne\varnothing\).

Conditional on \(n_z\), arm \(z\) is multinomial.  Its likelihood is therefore
\[
\frac{n_z!}{\prod_{t,y}N_{z,t,y}!\prod_{c,y}N_{z,c,y}!}
\prod_{t,y}s_z(t,y)^{N_{z,t,y}}
\prod_{c,y}\{s_z(\star)\eta_z(c,y)\}^{N_{z,c,y}}.
\]
Using \(S_{z,t,y}=N_{z,t,y}\) and \(S_{z,\star}=\sum_{c,y}N_{z,c,y}\), multiply and divide by \(S_{z,\star}!\).  With \(0^0=1\), the result is exactly
\[
\left[
\frac{n_z!}{\prod_{t,y}S_{z,t,y}!S_{z,\star}!}
\prod_{t,y}s_z(t,y)^{S_{z,t,y}}s_z(\star)^{S_{z,\star}}
\right]
\left[
\frac{S_{z,\star}!}{\prod_{c,y}N_{z,c,y}!}
\prod_{c,y}\eta_z(c,y)^{N_{z,c,y}}
\right]
=L_z(N_z;s_z,\eta_z).
\]
Randomization and conditional sampling make the arm likelihoods multiply, which proves the asserted product factorization.

Variation independence is constructive.  For every \(q\in\Delta^{|\mathcal R|-1}\) and every \(\eta\in\mathcal E_{\mathcal C}^m\), apply the armwise refinement with target probabilities \((Aq)_{z,(t,y)}\) and off-target probabilities \((Aq)_{z,\star}\eta_z(c,y)\).  This produces a full experiment with those parameters, including zero-star boundaries.  Hence the parameter space is the stated Cartesian product.

Finally, conditional on a skeleton table \(S=\sigma\), all target counts are fixed and the off-target counts in arm \(z\) have probability
\[
\frac{\sigma_{z,\star}!}{\prod_{c,y}N_{z,c,y}!}
\prod_{c,y}\eta_z(c,y)^{N_{z,c,y}},
\qquad \sum_{c,y}N_{z,c,y}=\sigma_{z,\star}.
\]
The multinomial theorem shows that these probabilities sum to one.  This conditional law involves \(\eta\) but not \(q\).  At \(\sigma_{z,\star}=0\) it is the point mass at the all-zero allocation, so the conclusion also holds on the boundary.
statements.justification: Factorization turns identification irrelevance into a precise statistical separation without falsely labeling the detailed counts ancillary.
statements.gap: Categorical instrumental-variable inference is written for the full multinomial law, and no located result isolates this variation-independent off-target allocation nuisance.
statements.consumer: Decision rules and confidence procedures can be designed on the skeleton experiment even when the data retain thousands of off-target labels.

statements.statement:
Suppose \(\mathcal C
e\varnothing\). Conditional on fixed finite arm counts \((n_z:z\in\mathcal Z)\), for every full-data rule \(\delta\), fixed nuisance point \(\eta^0\), and reduced law \(q\), the fiber \(\Omega(\sigma)=\{
u:S(
u)=\sigma\}\) is finite for every \(\sigma\), and \(\delta_0(\sigma)=\sum_{
u\in\Omega(\sigma)}K_{\eta^0}(
u\mid\sigma)\delta(
u)\in\mathcal A\). This rule satisfies \(R_q(\delta_0)\le R_{q,\eta^0}(\delta)\le\sup_\eta R_{q,\eta}(\delta)\). Conversely, every skeleton rule \(\phi\) lifts to the full-data rule \(\delta^{\phi}(
u)=\phi(S(
u))\), for which \(R_{q,\eta}(\delta^{\phi})=R_q(\phi)\) for all \(q,\eta\). Therefore \(\inf_\delta\sup_{q,\eta}R_{q,\eta}(\delta)=\inf_\phi\sup_qR_q(\phi)\). No pointwise inequality \(R_{q,\eta}(\delta_0)\le R_{q,\eta}(\delta)\) is asserted for arbitrary \(\eta\).
statements.proof_tex:
Assume \(\mathcal C\ne\varnothing\), so each fixed \(\eta^0_z\) is a probability distribution on the off-target cells. For fixed finite arm totals and any skeleton table \(\sigma\), each coordinate of a member of \(\Omega(\sigma)\) is an integer between zero and the corresponding \(n_z\). Hence \(\Omega(\sigma)\) is finite.  By the multinomial theorem applied separately in every arm,
\[
\sum_{\nu\in\Omega(\sigma)}K_{\eta^0}(\nu\mid\sigma)=1,
\qquad K_{\eta^0}(\nu\mid\sigma)\ge0.
\]
Thus \(\delta_0(\sigma)\) is a finite convex combination of points \(\delta(\nu)\in\mathcal A\).  Convexity of \(\mathcal A\) implies \(\delta_0(\sigma)\in\mathcal A\); no closure or limiting argument is needed.

The experiment factorization shows that under \((q,\eta^0)\), the conditional distribution of \(N\) given \(S=\sigma\) is precisely \(K_{\eta^0}(\cdot\mid\sigma)\), independently of \(q\).  Convexity of \(a\mapsto\ell(a,Bq)\) and finite Jensen therefore give, for every \(\sigma\),
\[
\ell(\delta_0(\sigma),Bq)
\le
\sum_{\nu\in\Omega(\sigma)}K_{\eta^0}(\nu\mid\sigma)
\ell(\delta(\nu),Bq).
\]
The marginal distribution of \(S\) depends on \(q\) through \(Aq\) and does not depend on \(\eta\).  Multiplying by this marginal probability and summing over \(\sigma\) gives
\[
R_q(\delta_0)
\le R_{q,\eta^0}(\delta)
\le\sup_{\eta\in\mathcal E_{\mathcal C}^m}R_{q,\eta}(\delta).
\]
The first inequality uses only the conditional law at the fixed point \(\eta^0\); it does not compare the two risks pointwise at an arbitrary \(\eta\).

Conversely, for a skeleton rule \(\phi\), define \(\delta^\phi(\nu)=\phi(S(\nu))\).  Since both its action and its target \(Bq\) are functions of the skeleton parameter and skeleton data alone,
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{q,\eta}(\delta^\phi)
 &=\sum_{\sigma}P_q(S=\sigma)\ell(\phi(\sigma),Bq)
   \sum_{\nu\in\Omega(\sigma)}K_\eta(\nu\mid\sigma)\\
 &=\sum_{\sigma}P_q(S=\sigma)\ell(\phi(\sigma),Bq)
 =R_q(\phi)
\end{aligned}
\]
for every \(q,\eta\).  Hence
\[
\inf_\phi\sup_qR_q(\phi)
\le\inf_\delta\sup_{q,\eta}R_{q,\eta}(\delta)
\]
by the first construction, while
\[
\inf_\delta\sup_{q,\eta}R_{q,\eta}(\delta)
\le\inf_\phi\sup_qR_q(\phi)
\]
by the lift.  The two minimax values are equal, with the inequalities valid as extended nonnegative real inequalities if a supremum is infinite.
statements.justification: Because fixed arm counts and finite alphabets make every \(\Omega(\sigma)\) finite, the barycenter exists for every rule and lies in the convex action space without closedness or integrability conditions; likelihood factorization makes \(K_{\eta^0}\) independent of \(q\), and Jensen's inequality gives the first risk bound.
statements.gap: Blackwell comparison does not directly apply because the conditional allocation kernel contains an unknown nuisance; the supremum over the variation-independent nuisance is the new step.
statements.consumer: A minimax analyst loses nothing by storing and processing only target cells and total off-target counts.

statements.statement: For every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), every \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathcal T,\mathcal C}\), and every off-target allocation \(\eta\), \(P\{\Theta(s)\subseteq\widehat\Theta_\alpha\mid(n_z)_z\}\ge1-\alpha\). The event follows from \(P\{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat s_z\|s_z)>\rho_z(\alpha)\}\le\alpha/m\) and therefore remains valid at endpoint kinks and simultaneously for every linear functional of \(\operatorname{law}(Y_{\mathcal T})\). Calibration and every optimization dimension are independent of \(|\mathcal C|\); direct response-type computation uses \((|\mathcal T|+1)^m2^{|\mathcal T|}\) columns and is exponential only in \(m\) and \(|\mathcal T|\).
statements.proof_tex:
Use the conventions \(0\log(0/a)=0\) and \(b\log(b/0)=+\infty\) for \(b>0\). For one unit in arm \(z\), the skeleton category has probabilities
\[
P\{J=(t,y)\mid Z=z\}=p_z(t,y)=s_z(t,y),
\qquad
P\{J=\star\mid Z=z\}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C,y}p_z(c,y)=s_z(\star).
\]
Hence, conditional on \(n_z\), \(S_z\sim\operatorname{Multinomial}(n_z,s_z)\). When \(\mathcal C=\varnothing\), \(s_z(\star)=0\) and \(S_{z,\star}=0\) almost surely, so the same multinomial type bound applies.

Fix an arm \(z\), abbreviate \(n_z\) by \(n_0\), and let \(r\) be an empirical type on the \(d\)-point skeleton alphabet.  Its exact multinomial probability under \(s_z\) is
\[
P_{s_z}(\widehat s_z=r)
=\frac{n_0!}{\prod_j(n_0r_j)!}\prod_js_{z,j}^{n_0r_j}.
\]
The multinomial expansion of \((\sum_jr_j)^{n_0}=1\) implies
\[
\frac{n_0!}{\prod_j(n_0r_j)!}\prod_jr_j^{n_0r_j}\le1,
\]
so
\[
P_{s_z}(\widehat s_z=r)
\le \exp\{-n_0D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r\|s_z)\}.
\]
There are at most \((n_0+1)^{d-1}\) types, because their first \(d-1\) integer counts determine the last count.  This method-of-types count yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{s_z}\{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat s_z\|s_z)>\rho_z(\alpha)\}
&\le(n_z+1)^{d-1}e^{-n_z\rho_z(\alpha)}\\
&=(n_z+1)^{d-1}
\exp\{-\log(m/\alpha)-(d-1)\log(n_z+1)\}\\
&=\alpha/m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Positive arm counts justify every division by \(n_z\).  Zero coordinates of \(s_z\) cause no problem: an empirical type charging such a coordinate has probability zero.

Define the simultaneous event
\[
\mathcal E_\alpha=
\bigcap_{z\in\mathcal Z}
\{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat s_z\|s_z)\le\rho_z(\alpha)\}.
\]
The union bound gives \(P(\mathcal E_\alpha\mid(n_z)_z)\ge1-\alpha\).  Quotient sharpness implies that the true skeleton belongs to \(\mathcal S\).  Therefore, on \(\mathcal E_\alpha\), \(s\in\mathcal K_\alpha(\widehat s)\), and the union defining the reported region contains its corresponding complete sharp set:
\[
\Theta(s)\subseteq
\bigcup_{s'\in\mathcal K_\alpha(\widehat s)}\Theta(s')
=\widehat\Theta_\alpha.
\]
The displayed skeleton multinomial law does not involve \(\eta\), so the probability bound is uniform over the off-target allocation nuisance.  The argument uses set inclusion only, not differentiability of an endpoint; it therefore remains valid at facet switches and simultaneously covers every linear functional of every \(\mu\in\Theta(s)\).

For computation, eliminate \(s'\) to obtain the explicit projection
\[
\widehat\Theta_\alpha
=\left\{Bq:q\in\Delta^{|\mathcal R|-1},\ 
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat s_z\|(Aq)_z)\le\rho_z(\alpha)
\text{ for all }z\in\mathcal Z\right\}.
\]
It has \((|\mathcal T|+1)^m2^{|\mathcal T|}\) response-type columns and \(md\) skeleton coordinates.  The radius contains only \(m,d,n_z,\alpha\).  Thus calibration and optimization are independent of \(|\mathcal C|\), while direct column enumeration is exponential in \(m\) and \(|\mathcal T|\).
statements.justification: The guarantee protects the complete sharp set in finite samples without selecting an active endpoint formula.
statements.gap: The theorem applies a reduced categorical method-of-types region after quotienting the target-only model, removing \(|\mathcal C|\) from calibration and computation; no published-model equivalence is asserted.
statements.consumer: Analysts with finely coded nonadherence or dosage deviations obtain honest whole-set uncertainty without merging scientific target levels.

statements.statement: The compatible-fiber modulus \(H_A\) is finite and admits a computable upper certificate obtained by enumerating the full-row-rank active submatrices of the equality-plus-nonnegativity system for \(F(s)\). For all \(s,s'\in\mathcal S\), \(e_1(\Theta(s'),\Theta(s))\le H_A\|s'-s\|_1\) and \(|h_{s'}(u)-h_s(u)|\le H_A\|u\|_\infty\|s'-s\|_1\). On the coverage event in Theorem 5, \(e_1(\widehat\Theta_\alpha,\Theta(s))\le2H_A\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt{2\rho_z(\alpha)}\). Every constant depends only on \(A\) and \(B\), hence on \(m\) and \(|\mathcal T|\), not on \(|\mathcal C|\).
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(C\) be a full-row-rank submatrix whose rows are a linearly independent subcollection spanning the row space of the augmented equality matrix, choosing \(\mathbf 1^\top\) as its first row,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf 1^\top\\ A\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For \(s\in\mathcal S\), let \(b(s)\) be the corresponding subvector of \((1,s)\). Since \((1,s)\) is compatible with all row relations of the augmented matrix,
\[
F(s)=\{q\ge0:Cq=b(s)\}.
\]
The cited fixed-matrix polyhedral feasible-fiber bound applies because every such fiber is a nonempty closed subset of the simplex and hence is bounded.  It supplies a finite, computable \(\overline H_A\), obtained from the finitely many full-row-rank active submatrices, such that
\[
e_1(F(s'),F(s))
\le\overline H_A\|b(s')-b(s)\|_1
\le\overline H_A\|s'-s\|_1.
\]
Taking the supremum in the definition of \(H_A\) proves \(H_A\le\overline H_A<\infty\) and gives the asserted computable upper certificate.

Every column of \(B\) contains exactly one entry equal to one.  Therefore, for every signed vector \(w\),
\[
\|Bw\|_1
\le\sum_y\sum_{r:y_{\mathcal T}(r)=y}|w_r|
=\|w\|_1.
\]
Fix \(\mu'=Bq'\in\Theta(s')\).  From the definition of directed excess, for every \(\epsilon>0\) there is \(q\in F(s)\) satisfying
\[
\|q'-q\|_1
\le e_1(F(s'),F(s))+\epsilon.
\]
It follows that
\[
\inf_{\mu\in\Theta(s)}\|\mu'-\mu\|_1
\le\|Bq'-Bq\|_1
\le H_A\|s'-s\|_1+\epsilon.
\]
Take the supremum over \(\mu'\) and then let \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) to obtain
\[
e_1(\Theta(s'),\Theta(s))\le H_A\|s'-s\|_1.
\]

Compactness of \(F(s)\) ensures that the support maximum is attained.  If \(q'\) maximizes \(u^\top Bq'\) over \(F(s')\), choose the preceding approximating \(q\in F(s)\).  Then
\[
h_{s'}(u)-h_s(u)
\le u^\top B(q'-q)
\le\|u\|_\infty\|B(q'-q)\|_1
\le H_A\|u\|_\infty\|s'-s\|_1+\|u\|_\infty\epsilon.
\]
Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) and interchanging \(s,s'\) proves the absolute-value inequality.

It remains to establish the confidence-width statement.  By the finite-alphabet Pinsker lemma, on the simultaneous event \(\mathcal E_\alpha\), whose probability guarantee follows from the direct skeleton multinomial argument in the finite-set coverage proof, every \(s'\in\mathcal K_\alpha(\widehat s)\) obeys, arm by arm,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|s'_z-s_z\|_1
&\le\|s'_z-\widehat s_z\|_1+\|\widehat s_z-s_z\|_1\\
&\le\sqrt{2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat s_z\|s'_z)}
 +\sqrt{2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat s_z\|s_z)}\\
&\le2\sqrt{2\rho_z(\alpha)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\|s'-s\|_1\le2\sum_z\sqrt{2\rho_z(\alpha)}\).  Apply the target-set excess inequality uniformly to every set in the union defining \(\widehat\Theta_\alpha\) to conclude
\[
e_1(\widehat\Theta_\alpha,\Theta(s))
\le2H_A\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt{2\rho_z(\alpha)}.
\]
The matrices \(A,B\), the active-submatrix list, and all displayed dimensions depend only on \(m\) and \(|\mathcal T|\).  No constant depends on the labels, allocation probabilities, or cardinality of \(\mathcal C\).
statements.justification: This converts sampling error in the reduced multinomial law into deterministic excess width for every target-law direction.
statements.gap: Hoffman and Li provide generic polyhedral sensitivity, but no published instrumental-variable result gives this compatible-simplex support modulus or its quotient-invariant confidence-width consequence.
statements.consumer: The bound supplies stopping rules, sample-size calculations, and numerical tolerances for projected target-law regions.

statements.statement: Suppose \(\mathcal C\ne\varnothing\). Under the interior, feasible-direction, regular-face, and nonzero-derivative conditions, there exist constants \(c>0\) and \(c_0>0\) such that \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sqrt n\inf_{\widehat h}\sup_{e\in\{-c,c\}}E_{s_0+ev/\sqrt n,\eta}|\widehat h-h_{s_0+ev/\sqrt n}(u_0)|\ge c_0\), even when \(\widehat h\) uses the full counts \(N\). The constants and the lower bound are uniform over off-target labels and all nonempty finite cardinalities of \(\mathcal C\).
statements.proof_tex:
Put
\[
a=\min_{z\in\mathcal Z,j\in\mathcal D}(s_0)_{z,j}>0,
\qquad
V=\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}v_{z,j}^2.
\]
The two-sided feasible-direction assumption implies \(\sum_jv_{z,j}=0\) for every arm. Moreover \(V>0\), because \(V=0\) would imply \(v=0\) and hence \(\gamma=0\), contrary to the nonzero-derivative assumption.

The stable unique nondegenerate optimal basis in the regular-face assumption remains primal and dual optimal in a neighborhood of \(s_0\).  The corresponding basic solution is affine in the equality right-hand side, so its objective value is affine.  Consequently there is \(\epsilon_1>0\) such that
\[
h_{s_0+\epsilon v}(u_0)=h_{s_0}(u_0)+\gamma\epsilon
\quad\text{whenever }|\epsilon|\le\epsilon_1.
\]
Choose a fixed \(c>0\) small enough that
\[
\frac{8c^2V}{a}\le\frac12.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(n\), feasibility of the two-sided direction gives \(s_{\pm,n}=s_0\pm cv/\sqrt n\in\mathcal S\), every coordinate of both laws is at least \(a/2\), and the local affine formula gives
\[
\Delta_n:=|h_{s_{+,n}}(u_0)-h_{s_{-,n}}(u_0)|
=\frac{2|\gamma|c}{\sqrt n}.
\]

Let \(P_{+,n}^{N,\eta}\) and \(P_{-,n}^{N,\eta}\) denote the conditional laws of the full counts at these two skeleton laws and the same arbitrary allocation \(\eta\).  Experiment factorization gives the same conditional kernel \(K_\eta(N\mid S)\) under both hypotheses.  The chain rule for the finite sum defining relative entropy therefore cancels that kernel and yields
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{+,n}^{N,\eta}\|P_{-,n}^{N,\eta})
=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}n_zD_{\mathrm{KL}}((s_{+,n})_z\|(s_{-,n})_z).
\]
For positive probability vectors \(p,q\), \(\log x\le x-1\) implies
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
\le\sum_j\frac{(p_j-q_j)^2}{q_j}.
\]
Using \((s_{+,n})_z-(s_{-,n})_z=2cv_z/\sqrt n\), the lower bound \((s_{-,n})_{z,j}\ge a/2\), and \(\sum_zn_z/n=1\), we obtain
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{+,n}^{N,\eta}\|P_{-,n}^{N,\eta})
\le\frac{8c^2}{a}\sum_z\frac{n_z}{n}\sum_jv_{z,j}^2
\le\frac{8c^2V}{a}\le\frac12.
\]
Within the stated nonempty-\(\mathcal C\) scope, this bound is uniform in \(\eta\), the off-target labels, and the finite cardinality.

The finite-alphabet Pinsker lemma gives
\[
\|P_{+,n}^{N,\eta}-P_{-,n}^{N,\eta}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le\sqrt{\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{+,n}^{N,\eta}\|P_{-,n}^{N,\eta})}
\le\frac12.
\]
For completeness, the two-point risk inequality follows directly.  With densities \(p_+,p_-\) relative to their sum and any full-count estimator \(\widehat h\), the triangle inequality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&E_+|\widehat h-h_{s_{+,n}}(u_0)|+E_-|\widehat h-h_{s_{-,n}}(u_0)|\\
&\quad\ge
\int\min(p_+,p_-)
\left(|\widehat h-h_{s_{+,n}}(u_0)|+|\widehat h-h_{s_{-,n}}(u_0)|\right)\\
&\quad\ge \Delta_n\int\min(p_+,p_-)
=\Delta_n\{1-\|P_{+,n}^{N,\eta}-P_{-,n}^{N,\eta}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
At least one of the two risks is therefore at least \(\Delta_n/4\).  Taking the infimum over all estimators, multiplying by \(\sqrt n\), and taking the lower limit yields
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sqrt n\inf_{\widehat h}
\sup_{e\in\{-c,c\}}E_{s_0+ev/\sqrt n,\eta}
|\widehat h-h_{s_0+ev/\sqrt n}(u_0)|
\ge\frac{|\gamma|c}{2}=:c_0>0.
\]
Both \(c\) and \(c_0\) use only \(s_0,v,\gamma,A,B\) and the reduced alphabet.  The cancellation of \(K_\eta\) proves uniformity over every off-target allocation, label set, and nonempty finite cardinality \(|\mathcal C|\).
statements.justification: The local two-point bound certifies that root-\(n\) width on a regular face cannot be improved by retaining off-target labels.
statements.gap: Existing endpoint work gives upper inference results or generic regularization, not a target-quotient lower bound uniform in off-target refinement.
statements.consumer: The result benchmarks the order of projected-region width and prevents claims that a larger off-target alphabet can improve regular-face rates.

statements.statement: Using the vanishing-penalty active-cone handle, characterize the local asymptotic minimax risk and limit experiment for \(h_s(u)\) at every skeleton law where the reduced dual program has multiple optimal vertices, and construct one data-driven estimator and confidence procedure that attains the resulting face-by-face frontier without knowing the active cone.
statements.justification: The exact behavior at facet switches is the first-class open content left after finite-sample coverage and regular-face optimality.
statements.gap: Levis et al. use margins or smoothing and Gafarov uses generic quadratic regularization; neither supplies the exact target-IV local minimax phase diagram.
statements.consumer: An attaining procedure would replace conservative whole-set projection by shorter calibrated intervals whenever the observed skeleton is near, but not exactly on, a dual tie.

obligation.what_is_open: The face-by-face local asymptotic minimax risk at every multiple-dual-vertex skeleton law, together with one data-driven confidence procedure that adapts uniformly to an unknown active cone.
obligation.obstruction: The frozen core does not specify the local parameter set, loss, or confidence criterion needed to define a unique local asymptotic minimax risk.  More substantively, at sequences approaching a dual tie at the root-\(n\) scale, active-cone selection is nonuniform; the deterministic directional envelope alone does not prove that vanishing quadratic regularization attains a common frontier over all such sequences.
obligation.attempted: Reduced the support function to its finite polyhedral dual envelope, isolated its directional derivative at a multiple optimum, and examined the Gaussian-shift route suggested by the vanishing-penalty handle.  The remaining step is a uniform limit experiment for feasible projection plus a lower and upper minimax match over drifting active cones.
obligation.partial_result:
After redundant equality rows are removed, write the reduced primal program as
\[
h_s(u)=\max_{q\ge0}\{(B^\top u)^\top q:Cq=b(s)\}.
\]
Its dual is the finite-dimensional polyhedral program
\[
h_s(u)=\min_{\beta}\{\beta^\top b(s):C^\top\beta\ge B^\top u\}.
\]
On any neighborhood on which the value is finite, this is the lower envelope of the affine functions associated with the finitely many relevant dual vertices.  If \(\Lambda_0(u)\) is the set of vertices optimal at \(s_0\), then for every feasible direction \(v\), polyhedral envelope algebra gives the one-sided directional derivative
\[
h'_{s_0}(u;v)=\min_{\beta\in\Lambda_0(u)}\beta^\top \dot b(v).
\]
Indeed, vertices not optimal at \(s_0\) have a strictly positive objective gap and cannot minimize for sufficiently small positive perturbations, while taking the minimum over the vertices in \(\Lambda_0(u)\) gives the displayed first-order coefficient.  Thus a multiple-vertex point has a computable piecewise-linear first-order map, and unequal active slopes are exactly the first-order kink.  This establishes the deterministic local envelope, but it does not by itself determine a minimax risk or an adaptive confidence law.

statements.statement: Let \(C\) be a fixed full-row-rank real matrix whose first row is \(\mathbf 1^\top\), and let \(G(b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:Cx=b,\ x\ge0\}\).  Over all right-hand sides whose first coordinate is one and whose fiber is nonempty, there is a finite constant \(H(C)\) such that \(e_1(G(b'),G(b))\le H(C)\|b'-b\|_1\).  A valid upper constant is computable from the finitely many full-row-rank active submatrices of the equality-plus-nonnegativity system (equivalently, after replacing each equality by two inequalities).

source.locator: Sections 2--3, feasible-solution Lipschitz constants for a perturbed linear program
source.verbatim_statement: The purpose of this paper is to derive the sharp Lipschitz constants for the feasible solutions and optimal solutions of a linear program with respect to right-hand-side perturbations. The Lipschitz constants are given in terms of pseudoinverses of submatrices of the matrices involved and are proven to be sharp.

statements.statement:
For probability vectors \(a,b\) on the same finite alphabet, with relative entropy defined by \(0\log(0/b_j)=0\) and \(a_j\log(a_j/0)=+\infty\) when \(a_j>0\),
\[
\|a-b\|_1\le\sqrt{2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|b)}.
\]
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(E=\{j:a_j\ge b_j\}\) and \(t=a(E)-b(E)=\|a-b\|_1/2\).  Convexity of \(x\mapsto x\log x\), applied separately on \(E\) and its complement, gives the log-sum reduction
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|b)\ge d_{\mathrm{bin}}(a(E)\|b(E)).
\]
For fixed \(r\in(0,1)\), the second derivative in \(x\) of \(d_{\mathrm{bin}}(x\|r)\) is \(1/[x(1-x)]\ge4\), while its value and first derivative vanish at \(x=r\).  Taylor's integral formula gives
\[
d_{\mathrm{bin}}(x\|r)\ge2(x-r)^2.
\]
Boundary cases follow by taking limits; if the relative entropy is infinite the desired inequality is immediate.  Consequently
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a\|b)\ge2t^2=\tfrac12\|a-b\|_1^2,
\]
which is equivalent to the claim.

statements.statement:
Let \(\pi_{yd.z}\ge 0\), indexed by \(y,d,z\in\{0,1\}\), satisfy \(\sum_{y,d}\pi_{yd.z}=1\) for each \(z\). Suppose that the binary instrumental-variable response-type fiber
\[
 \mathcal Q_{\mathrm{IV}}(\pi)
 =\left\{\widetilde q\in\Delta^{15}:
 \pi_{yd.z}=\sum_{d_0,d_1,u_0,u_1}\widetilde q_{d_0d_1u_0u_1}
 \mathbf 1\{d_z=d,\ u_d=y\}\ \text{for all }y,d,z\right\}
\]
is nonempty. For
\[
 \operatorname{ACE}(\widetilde q)
 =\sum_{d_0,d_1,u_0,u_1}\widetilde q_{d_0d_1u_0u_1}(u_1-u_0),
\]
the minimum over \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{IV}}(\pi)\) equals
\[
L_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)=\max\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{11.1}-1,\\
&\pi_{00.1}+\pi_{11.1}-1,\\
&\pi_{11.0}+\pi_{00.1}-1,\\
&\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{11.0}-1,\\
&2\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{11.0}+\pi_{10.1}+\pi_{11.1}-2,\\
&\pi_{00.0}+2\pi_{11.0}+\pi_{00.1}+\pi_{01.1}-2,\\
&\pi_{10.0}+\pi_{11.0}+2\pi_{00.1}+\pi_{11.1}-2,\\
&\pi_{00.0}+\pi_{01.0}+\pi_{00.1}+2\pi_{11.1}-2
\end{aligned}\right\},
\]
and the maximum equals
\[
U_{\mathrm{BP}}(\pi)=\min\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&1-\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{01.1},\\
&1-\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{10.1},\\
&1-\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{10.0},\\
&1-\pi_{01.1}-\pi_{10.1},\\
&2-2\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{10.1}-\pi_{11.1},\\
&2-\pi_{01.0}-2\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{00.1}-\pi_{01.1},\\
&2-\pi_{10.0}-\pi_{11.0}-2\pi_{01.1}-\pi_{10.1},\\
&2-\pi_{00.0}-\pi_{01.0}-\pi_{01.1}-2\pi_{10.1}
\end{aligned}\right\}.
\]
Both extrema are attainable by response-type distributions in \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{IV}}(\pi)\).

statements.statement: Gabriel, Sachs, and Sj\"olander report that, for a two-level instrument with two well-defining exposure levels and one potentially ill-defining level under NPSEM (2.5), the tight valid bounds for the specified target contrast have the same expression as the familiar two-level-IV bounds. They also report that, for a three-level instrument and two well-defining exposure levels under NPSEM (2.2), the tight valid bounds have the same expression as those obtained after allowing a third potentially ill-defining level.

For a three-level IV and two well-defining levels of the coarsened exposure X, under NPSEM (2.2), the tight and valid bounds have that same expression as those allowing for a third potentially ill-defining level.

statements.statement: Define an internal one-off-target structural class by a finite latent response type \(U=(x_{\mathcal Z},y_{\mathcal T},r_{c,\mathcal Z})\), independent randomized assignment \(Z\), common target responses \(Y_t=y_t(U)\), exposure responses \(X_z=x_z(U)\), and arm-specific off-target responses \(R_{c,z}=r_{c,z}(U)\). This structural class and the full response-type class with \(\mathcal C=\{c\}\) induce exactly the same laws of \((X_{\mathcal Z},Y_{\mathcal T},R_{c,\mathcal Z})\), hence preserve the observed arm law \(p\) and \(\operatorname{law}(Y_{\mathcal T})\). The same response types also admit an internal fine-version representation with fine labels \((c,z)\) coarsened to \(c\). No equivalence with a published NPSEM class is asserted.
statements.proof_tex:
The forward map simply records the internally defined coordinates
\[
(X_{\mathcal Z},Y_{\mathcal T},R_{c,\mathcal Z})
=(x_{\mathcal Z}(U),y_{\mathcal T}(U),r_{c,\mathcal Z}(U)).
\]
Because \(Z\) is independent of \(U\), it is independent of this finite response vector. Setting \(X=X_Z\) and using \(Y_t\) on target branches and \(R_{c,Z}\) on the off-target branch gives the incidence identities
\[
P(X=t,Y=y\mid Z=z)=P(X_z=t,Y_t=y),\qquad
P(X=c,Y=y\mid Z=z)=P(X_z=c,R_{c,z}=y),
\]
so the observed arm law and the complete target law are determined by the recorded response-type law.

Conversely, given any probability law on the full response-type space with \(\mathcal C=\{c\}\), take the full response type itself as \(U\), take auxiliary errors to be degenerate, and draw \(Z\) independently with the stated positive arm probabilities. The displayed structural equations then reproduce every response coordinate exactly.

For the internal fine-version representation, use the finite support
\[
\mathcal X^*=\mathcal T\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{(c,z):z\in\mathcal Z\},
\]
coarsen each \(t\) to itself and every \((c,z)\) to \(c\), and, on an off-target branch in arm \(z\), select fine version \((c,z)\) with outcome \(r_{c,z}(U)\). This again reproduces the same response vector coordinatewise. Thus the two internally defined representations have identical response-law fibers and target-law images. The construction is self-contained and makes no claim about the scope of any cited published model.

statements.statement: Song, Guo, Chan, and Richardson consider categorical outcome, treatment, and instrument variables, assume the existence of potential outcomes \(Y(x=i,z=q)\), and define \(Y(x):=Y(x,Z)\) as the potential outcome arising from an intervention on \(X\) alone.

source.verbatim_statement: Consider a categorical outcome Y with M at least 2 levels, a treatment variable X with K at least 2 levels, and an instrumental variable Z with Q at least 1 levels. For all the models we consider, we will assume the existence of potential outcomes Y(x=i,z=q) for i in [K], q in [Q]. We also define Y(x) := Y(x,Z) to be the potential outcome for Y arising from an intervention on X alone.

statements.statement:
Define the internal finite response-type space
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{AI}}=\mathcal X^{\mathcal Z}\times\mathcal Y^{\mathcal X}.
\]
The map sending \((x_{\mathcal Z},(y_x)_{x\in\mathcal X})\) to
\[
\bigl(x_{\mathcal Z},(y_t)_{t\in\mathcal T},
(r_{c,z}=y_c)_{c\in\mathcal C,z\in\mathcal Z}\bigr)
\]
is a bijection onto the subset of \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm F}\) with arm-invariant off-target responses. Its affine extension preserves the internally defined observed incidence map and target-law map. This is a finite-set algebraic identity; no equivalence with a cited published model is asserted.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(z_0\in\mathcal Z\). On a full response type with \(r_{c,z}=r_{c,z'}\) for all \(c,z,z'\), define the inverse by retaining \(x_{\mathcal Z}\), taking \(y_t\) from the target coordinates, and setting \(y_c=r_{c,z_0}\). Arm invariance makes the last definition independent of \(z_0\). Both compositions are coordinatewise identities, proving bijectivity.

For a law \(\omega\) on \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{AI}}\), define
\[
(A_{\mathrm{AI}}\omega)_{z,(x,y)}
=\sum_g\omega_g\mathbf 1\{x_z(g)=x,\ y_x(g)=y\}.
\]
If \(\pi\) is the pushforward law, the defining map gives \(y_t\) on a target branch and \(r_{c,z}=y_c\) on an off-target branch. Hence
\[
(A_{\mathrm F}\pi)_{z,(x,y)}=(A_{\mathrm{AI}}\omega)_{z,(x,y)}
\]
for every cell. The map also retains \((y_t)_{t\in\mathcal T}\) coordinatewise, so its affine extension preserves the target-law map. These conclusions follow solely from the displayed finite-set definitions.
